label: Title
notes: Open with the contract for this chapter: curvature will be read from metric comparisons rather than from derivatives of a tensor. Name the provenance explicitly. The deck follows the chapter-four notebook and the assigned source span, printed pages 101 through 134 and PDF pages 116 through 149. The phrase without smoothness is the organizing promise.

label: Chapter Question
notes: Pose the chapter question before giving definitions. Students know geodesics and constructions; now the task is to decide when a space is no fatter or no thinner than a model plane. The important move is that every test uses distances among points on geodesic triangles, so it still makes sense in polyhedral, cone, and branching examples.

label: Comparison Dictionary
notes: Treat the comparison triangle as a dictionary. A triangle in the metric space is translated into a Euclidean or model-space triangle with the same three side lengths, then points on corresponding sides are compared. Emphasize that the comparison triangle is not an embedding of the original triangle; it is a measuring instrument.

label: Two Inequality Directions
notes: Slow down the inequality directions. Upper curvature bounds and lower curvature bounds are easy to reverse by memory, so attach them to the visual language: CAT upper-bound triangles are not thicker than the model, while CBB lower-bound triangles are not thinner than the model. The same residual plot can be read as evidence for which side wins.

label: Local Definitions
notes: Local definitions are tests carried out in sufficiently small balls. The point is not to demand one global model triangle for a whole space, but to make every small geodesic triangle pass the correct comparison. Mention that the chapter later discusses how local information can globalize under extra hypotheses.

label: Fan CAT Example
notes: Use the fan as the first positive CAT example. A Euclidean fan glued along a spine can still make triangle distances contract relative to the flat comparison triangle, because geodesics can share a central hinge. The example helps students see why nonsmooth does not mean uncontrolled.

label: L1 Plane Warning
notes: The L1 plane is the warning label. It has straight-looking geodesics and a familiar topology, but the norm creates many geodesics and the comparison tests fail in characteristic ways. This prevents students from equating metric vector spaces with Euclidean local curvature behavior.

label: Equivalence Route
notes: This slide is the proof-route map. Present the equivalence theorem as a network of tests: distance comparison, midpoint or quadrilateral inequalities, angle behavior, and convexity of distance functions. The diagram is useful because no single definition has to carry all intuition at once.

label: Angle Existence
notes: Angles have to be earned in a metric space. Explain that the angle between geodesics is recovered as a limiting comparison angle, not assumed from an inner product. The teaching emphasis is existence and compatibility: once comparison controls small triangles, the limiting angle becomes a stable local datum.

label: Distance Sensors
notes: Distance functions are sensors because they convert geometric curvature into one-variable inequalities along geodesics. Rather than staring at all triangles at once, measure how the distance to a fixed point changes along a moving geodesic. Convexity or concavity is then a readable trace of the curvature bound.

label: E Convexity
notes: Introduce E-convexity and E-concavity as error-corrected versions of ordinary convexity. The correction term accounts for the model curvature and the fact that distance squared is the natural smooth proxy. Students should hear that the sign of the inequality records the same upper-versus-lower curvature split from earlier.

label: First Variation
notes: First variation connects the metric chapter back to the familiar differential-geometric formula. The rate of change of distance along a geodesic is controlled by the cosine of the angle at the base point. In this nonsmooth setting the statement is still about comparison angles and one-sided derivatives.

label: Numerical First Variation
notes: Use the numerical residual as a sanity check rather than as a proof. The plot asks whether finite differences of distance agree with the angle predicted by the first-variation formula. It gives students a concrete diagnostic for when the theorem is saying something measurable.

label: Nonzero Bounds
notes: The zero-curvature story generalizes by replacing the Euclidean comparison triangle with a model triangle in the constant-curvature plane. Positive, zero, and negative model geometries change angle sums and distance behavior, but the logical structure of comparison remains the same.

label: Globalization Roadmap
notes: Globalization should be framed as a roadmap, not a magic theorem. Local comparison requires completeness, geodesic control, and topological hypotheses before it can become a global statement. The chapter uses this to explain why curvature bounds are both local tests and global geometry theorems.

label: Cone Curvature Lab
notes: Close with cones because they tie the chapter back to constructions. Cone angle controls concentrated curvature at the tip: small total angle behaves positively, the Euclidean angle is flat, and excess angle behaves negatively. The linked cone-angle lab is the take-home inspection tool for the same idea.
